cim: Is Artificial Intelligence the New Third Wheel in Relationships?
cim_eredeti: Is Artificial Intelligence the New Third Wheel in Relationships?
szoveg_eredeti:
You’ve just had an argument with your partner. It’s late, you’re upset, and a message sits in your drafts, rewritten several times. You’re not sure whether you’re being unreasonable, whether you owe them an apology, or whether they owe you one. So, instead of calling a friend, you open a chatbot, attach screenshots, and ask: Am I overreacting?

It listens without interrupting or becoming defensive. It doesn’t bring up something from three months ago or ask for space midway through a difficult conversation. And it’s always available.

It sounds like the ideal partner. Except it isn’t your partner. It’s artificial intelligence.

And if you think AI’s growing presence in our romantic lives is merely confined to decoding messages and drafting apologies, consider the Substack essay that went viral: I Stumbled Across My Boyfriend’s ChatGPT and It Ended Our Relationship. Writer Lindsey Hall recounts how discovering her boyfriend’s private ChatGPT conversations about their relationship ultimately contributed to their breakup. AI is no longer just helping us navigate our relationships; it is increasingly becoming part of them. And as AI finds its way into our romantic lives, it’s worth asking what makes it such an appealing confidant in the first place.

Love has always come with uncertainties and, unfortunately, no instruction manual. Traditionally, we’ve turned to friends, siblings, and occasionally our own questionable judgement to make sense of it all. Now, artificial intelligence is becoming another sounding board for matters of the heart.

And the numbers suggest this is more than just a passing trend. According to Kantar’s global research, 54% of consumers across the markets surveyed had used AI for at least one emotional or mental wellbeing purpose. A separate Global Dialogues study, involving participants across 70 countries, found that 48.2% turned to AI for emotional support or personal issues at least once a week. The appeal of AI is extending beyond everyday questions to some of our most personal dilemmas.

For some, AI offers a space to process thoughts they haven’t found the courage to share with their partners; for others, it provides an outside perspective before making a decision. Relationship and sex therapist Georgina Vass says its appeal lies in the emotional convenience it offers. “AI is appealing because, unlike friends or loved ones, it’s discreet, non-judgemental, and entirely selfless,” she explains. It allows people to explore private matters while preserving their dignity, without the vulnerability that often comes with human interaction.

The question isn’t whether we should turn to AI for relationship advice, but how much of our emotional lives we’re willing to hand over. The trouble begins when the second opinion becomes the only opinion we trust.

Relationship coach Ruchi Ruuh draws a distinction between being non-judgemental and being subservient. AI, she argues, offers emotional convenience rather than the kind of understanding we might find in human interactions. “When we interact with humans we face resistance, autonomy, boredom or lack of enthusiasm. All these things help us understand ourselves better.”

Unlike human relationships, AI removes much of that complexity. While this can make conversations easier, Ruuh believes it can also make them less meaningful. “All these things that look like work in favour of a conversation actually make it bland.”

Vass, meanwhile, sees AI as a useful tool for preparing for difficult conversations but cautions against relying on it to resolve conflicts. “People are relational, and relational skills are generally developed through practice not data.”

Convenience, then, should not be mistaken for connection. AI might help us draft the perfect reply, but knowing what to say is only one part of being in a relationship. The harder part is knowing how to listen, when to compromise, and how to show up for another person. Which brings us to a bigger question.

Take Vidya, for instance, whose suspicions about her fiancé have been growing. After an argument, she turned to an AI chatbot to help frame questions that might encourage him to open up without making her suspicions too obvious. Soon, AI was helping her figure out not just what to say, but how to confront someone she was supposed to trust.

There’s another complication when we turn to AI with our relationship troubles: it hears only the side of the story we choose to tell. What we leave out can shape the advice we receive. Ruuh points to the risk of confirmation bias, explaining that AI can reinforce our existing beliefs when it responds solely to the information provided. It can become “an echo chamber for their thoughts”, offering validation without encouraging us to consider our own role in a conflict or our partner’s perspective.

AI can help us find the right words and navigate difficult conversations, but love has never been about getting everything right. It is about being vulnerable, making mistakes, and learning along the way. A machine can help us make sense of love, but it cannot experience it for us. For all the answers AI may offer, love is still something we have to learn by being in it.
